catalog_quote: Rukiga has two basic tones, high (H) and low (L). H is indicated with an acute accent mark over the vowel (á), and L is unmarked. Falling tone (F), marked with a circumflex over the vowel (â), appears. Rising tone (R) does not appear. [...] H tone does not appear every time as H. Characteristically, it becomes F in penultimate heavy syllables in utterance-final position, as in (3). [...] Notably, F tone appears only on the heavy penultimate syllable of words. It never appears on the antepenultimate or more left syllable of words, even though the syllable has a long vowel. It does not appear on the final syllable of words either because the final syllable of words does not accommodate two moras in Rukiga. [fn. 3, p. 30:] We do not consider the theoretical question of whether the opposition is either H vs. L or H vs. Ø. Simply, H and L are used. In this paper, the term “tone” is used both…

sweep_summary: Chiga (chig1238) is not in the catalog. All three title-keyword items are print-only: (1) Philippson 1991/92 thesis (Paris 5, 542 pp; Glottolog links it to Chiga among ~50 East African Bantu languoids) - only the theses.fr abstract is online, which frames the survey as running from purely tonal systems to purely demarcative penultimate stress, with the emergence of penultimate accent as the hypothesised driver of change; the Chiga-specific classification was not seen; priority medium. (2) Johnson 1976 'Devoicing, tone and stress in Runyankore' (SCOPIL 3, pp. 207-216) - HathiTrust search-only, no Google Books preview; describes Runyankore (nyan1307), the sister variety in the Nkore-Kiga cluster; the most likely explicit statement on stress for this cluster; priority high. (3) Ohly 1982 (Kiswahili 49: 93-97) on stress assimilation of Swahili/Oriental loanwords in Runyankore - HathiTrust search-only, AJOL only from vol. 70; secondary loanword evidence; priority medium. No first-hand word-stress statement for Chiga was read in this search of works with stress in the title (no new stress statement was found); the open Rukiga/Runyankore literature already held by the project (Kaji, Yukawa, Hyman, Poletto, Van der Wal & Asiimwe, Asiimwe) describes a H/L tone system with utterance-final penultimate falling tone on heavy syllables and no word-final phonetic lengthening (Kaji 2024), but says nothing about stress placement. StressTyp2 has no Nkore-Kiga entry.fr, HAL, HathiTrust bib API, Open Library, archive.org, Crossref, Glottolog and StressTyp2 directly.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Rukiga is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with lexically placed H; no word stress is described. Prosodic prominence effects are tonal and positional: a lexical H on a heavy penultimate syllable is realised as falling before pause, and the H of a word-final or penultimate syllable is anticipated (shifted leftward) in isolation. The sister variety Runyankore (Hyman 2020, p. 53) is likewise a privative /H/ vs Ø system in which a prepausal final H is retracted onto the penult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Kaji notes northern vs southern Rukiga dialect differences in tone (Section 6) and that Runyankore lacks the two-H nominals and penultimate-H anticipation of Rukiga; Yukawa 2002 (p. 2) reports Taylor's 'Low Speakers' vs 'High Speakers' distinction in Kiga/Nkore tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone patterns given for nouns in isolation; the F-tone realisation and the anticipation rule are stated for utterance-final (prepausal) position, i.e. phrase-level conditioning on word tone. No source opened uses the word 'stress' for Rukiga or Runyankore.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Kaji 2024) describes Rukiga proper, mainly the southern dialect around Lake Bunyonyi (Kabale), i.e. Chiga chig1238; Kaji notes tonal differences between northern and southern Rukiga and between Rukiga and Runyankore. The Hyman 2020/2023 and Poletto 1996/1998 items describe Runyankore (Nyankore, Glottolog nyan1307), the closely related variety usually grouped with Rukiga as 'Runyankore-Rukiga' (Taylor's 'Nkore-Kiga'); Yukawa 2002 describes Kiga from a Kabale-raised speaker. Van der Wal & Asiimwe 2020 and Asiimwe 2024 are Rukiga (JE14).

sources.note: 'Accent' = tone: acute for H, circumflex for falling, unmarked L (existence of falling doubtful). sources.quote: This work studies the very diverse prosodic systems of east African bantu languages, on the basis of non-linear (autosegmental and metrical) phonology. We find a one end purely tonal systems (like kikuyu) and at the other end systems with purely demarcative penultimate stress, with all intermediate cases. [...] a hypothesis is presented according to which the emergence of penultimate accent is the main cause of the evolution of these systems.
sources.note: Comparative tone/accent survey of ~50 East African Bantu languages including Chiga (Glottolog ref 38907); likely to classify Nkore-Kiga as tonal vs accentual and to note any penultimate prominence. theses.fr 1992PA05H011 records it as not accessible online.
